newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rainy German weather helps winter crops.
newsitem.headline: Rainy German weather helps winter crops.

text.p: Cloudy and wet weather forecast in Germany over the next seven days will aid newly sown 1997 crops but will damage 1996 crops still in the ground.

"It will be be good for the newly-sown winter barley and rapeseed crops, which will be followed by rye and wheat, but it is damaging for the delayed 1996 harvests," a DWD meteorological office source said.
Large grain acreages in the south-eastern German states of Thuringia and Saxony are still not harvested and maize, potato, fruit and wine harvests were also generally late.
The quality of late wheat and rye was deteriorating fast, with grain sprouting and weeds developing in wet fields, a weather expert in Lower Saxony state said.
This could impair the soil quality for forthcoming winter and spring crops.
Early night frosts could also threaten winter crops as well as damage remaining 1996 crop maize, which is exclusively used for pig and beef feed in this northern state.
Maximum national day temperatures should be 15 degrees Celsius over the next week after averages of 10 to 17 over the last seven days, the DWD institute said.
In south-eastern Germany, too much rain and lack of sunshine in the early part of the summer caused harvesting delays, which depressed the quality of wheat and rye.
Grain analyst Peter Gerl at the Berlin office of farm price institute ZMP said winter rapeseed was developing favourably but winter grain sowings were delayed.
Designated winter grain areas might have to be sown to spring crops in 1997 if soil quality did not recover or if night frosts set in too early this year.

Gerl also said a Bonn farm ministry estimate a month ago of a 12.8 million tonne crop in eastern Germany this year (13.6 million 1995) may be optimistic as it assumed all sown areas would be harvested.
While western Germany might raise its 1996 average grain yield to 6.5 tonnes per hectare from 6.2 tph last year, eastern Germany's might drop to 5.3 from 6.0.
East Germany would seek to export its surplus grain to eastern neighbours as western European markets were dominated by French and British sellers, Gerl said.

The national state quality assessment centre in Detmold said its annual grain crop report, due at the end of September, would be delayed by up to four weeks because samples had been received late and in widely varying qualities. --Vera Eckert, Hamburg newsroom, +49-40-41903275
